titulo: Cenário 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude (banco de treino)

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma is building a developer-productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK, and the agent loads the monorepo's root and package-level CLAUDE.md files as standing instructions. When it generates endpoint boilerplate in `batch-records/`, it applies the GxP audit-trail standards kept in `docs/standards/gxp-audit.md`. In `trials/`, it follows that package's naming rules but generates endpoints with no audit-trail fields, and when asked, it says it was given no audit standards. `batch-records/CLAUDE.md` contains the line `@../docs/standards/gxp-audit.md`; `trials/CLAUDE.md` says 'For audit trails, follow the rules in docs/standards/gxp-audit.md.' What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The `trials/` file is a directory-level CLAUDE.md, which the agent consults for files it reads but not for files it creates, so the audit rule is skipped.
The standards file is too long to load next to the package's own rules, so the agent keeps the short naming rules and drops the longer audit document.
Only `batch-records/CLAUDE.md` uses `@import` syntax, which pulls the file's content into context; the sentence in `trials/CLAUDE.md` names the file but never loads it.
The audit rule in `trials/CLAUDE.md` conflicts with the root CLAUDE.md, and the agent resolves such conflicts by keeping the root-level instruction over the package-level one.
questoes.explicacao: An `@path` import is how a CLAUDE.md pulls another file's content into context, which keeps each package's CLAUDE.md modular while sharing common standards. A sentence that merely mentions a path is plain text: the agent sees the instruction but not the standards themselves, which is why `trials/` follows its inline naming rules yet knows nothing about audit trails. Replacing the sentence with an `@import` of the standards file fixes it.
feedbacks: Tempting because directory-level files load contextually, but `trials/CLAUDE.md` is clearly loaded: its naming rules are applied during generation. What differs is how the audit file is referenced.

Tempting because long context can crowd out instructions, but `batch-records/` loads the very same document without trouble. The audit rules are missing in `trials/` because that file never imports them.
Correct. `@import` brings the standards file's content into context; a prose mention of the path does not.
Instruction conflicts do cause inconsistent behavior, but nothing in the root file is about audit trails, and the agent says it received no audit standards at all, which points to a missing import.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, automates repetitive upgrades: a coordinator assigns one service at a time to a `migrator` subagent, which edits files and runs the build through Bash. On any failure the subagent returns `{"status": "error", "message": "Migration failed for <service>"}`. Last week the coordinator marked 6 of 31 services as 'incompatible with the new logging library'. Engineers later found that 4 of them had failed only because the internal package registry timed out, after most of their files had already been migrated. What is the main flaw in this design?
opcoes: Any subagent failure should stop the whole run, so that an engineer can inspect the repository before the coordinator draws conclusions about compatibility.
The subagent should retry the build with backoff and, if it keeps failing, report the service as skipped so that the remaining services keep moving.
The coordinator should re-run each failed service from a clean checkout, so that partially migrated files do not get mixed with the original code.
The error has no failure type, no record of the command attempted and no partial results, so the coordinator cannot tell a registry timeout from any real incompatibility.
questoes.explicacao: A coordinator can recover intelligently only when the subagent reports what kind of failure occurred, what it attempted, what it had already completed and which alternatives exist. Here a transient registry timeout and a genuine incompatibility produce the same generic message, so the coordinator draws the wrong conclusion and discards migrated work. A structured error such as `{failure_type: 'transient', attempted: 'mvn package', completed: ['core', 'api'], alternatives: ['retry after the registry recovers']}` lets it retry or resume instead.
feedbacks: Terminating the whole workflow on a single failure is an anti-pattern: 25 services were fine, and the four registry timeouts only needed a retry. Stopping everything also gives the coordinator no better information.

Local retry for transient failures is good practice, but ending with a generic 'skipped' status repeats the core problem: the coordinator still cannot tell why the service failed or what was already migrated.
Starting from a clean checkout throws away the work that had succeeded and still leaves the coordinator guessing at the cause, so the same misclassification would happen on the next run.
Correct. Structured error context (type, attempted command, partial results, alternatives) is what lets the coordinator choose to retry, resume or report a real incompatibility.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, connects to an MCP server that queries the legacy LIMS test database so engineers can understand old data flows. Results sometimes include trial subject identifiers, so the team registered a PostToolUse hook that replaces any value matching `SUBJ-\d{6}` with `[REDACTED]`. Server logs show the server returned 214 raw identifiers last week, yet no agent answer or reasoning trace contains one. An engineer suspects the hook only cleans the transcript after the model has already seen the raw values. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The engineer is right: PostToolUse runs after the model has consumed the result, so it can clean what is logged and displayed but not what the model reasons over.
The redaction works only because the server marks those results with `isError`, which makes the SDK pass them through the hook before they reach the model.
PostToolUse fires only for built-in tools such as Read and Bash, so MCP results bypass the hook and the redaction must be happening inside the MCP server.
PostToolUse intercepts the tool result after the tool runs and before the model processes it, so the model only ever reasons over the redacted version.
questoes.explicacao: A PostToolUse hook sits between tool execution and the model: it receives the tool's output and can transform it before that output is added to the conversation. That is why the server logs show raw identifiers while nothing the model produces contains them. The same interception point is used to normalize formats or trim fields returned by MCP tools before the agent reasons over them.
feedbacks: This reverses the order. The hook acts on the result before it is appended to the conversation, so the model never receives the raw identifiers in the first place.
`isError` signals a failed tool call and has nothing to do with whether hooks run. These were successful results, processed by PostToolUse because the hook matches the tool.

Tempting because built-in tools are the classic example, but PostToolUse also applies to MCP tool results; normalizing data from MCP tools is a standard use. The server logs show it returns raw values.
Correct. PostToolUse transforms the tool result before the model processes it, which is why raw identifiers appear in server logs but never in the agent's reasoning.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, supports both plan mode and direct execution. An engineer asks it to replace the LIMS's 12-year-old SFTP file-drop integration with laboratory instruments. Two approaches are on the table: a message queue, which needs new broker infrastructure, or a REST ingestion API behind the existing gateway. Either one touches about 30 files in four modules. A teammate proposes direct execution: 'git makes rollback cheap, so let the agent pick an approach and we will review the diff.' How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: reviewing the final diff gives the same safety as planning, and git makes a wrong architectural choice cheap to undo before anything gets merged to main.
Reject it: choosing between approaches with different infrastructure needs is an architectural decision, so plan mode should explore and settle the design first.
Accept it, but split the work into four direct-execution runs, one per module, so that each diff stays small enough for the team to review carefully.
Reject it: changes spanning four modules should be written by engineers by hand, with the agent limited to answering questions about the existing code.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode is meant for tasks with architectural implications, multiple valid approaches and multi-file changes: here the agent must compare two integrations with different infrastructure requirements before touching about 30 files. Exploring and agreeing on the design first prevents costly rework; once the approach is chosen, direct execution can implement it. Letting the agent pick an approach mid-edit buries the most important decision inside a large diff.
feedbacks: A diff review happens after the cost is paid: by then the agent has committed to one integration and edited 30 files. Rollback restores the code, not the time, and the team never compared the approaches.
Correct. A choice between integration approaches with different infrastructure needs is what plan mode is for; direct execution can follow once the design is agreed.
Smaller diffs help review, but splitting by module still leaves the agent to choose the architecture implicitly, possibly differently in each run. The decision must come before the work is divided.
This pushes the work back onto engineers instead of using the agent well. Large architectural changes call for plan mode, not for abandoning the agent.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma engineers use the team's Agent SDK productivity agent to generate boilerplate for new LIMS modules. Reviewing a generated stability-sample module, an engineer finds four problems: the entity stores sample times as local time, the mapper converts to UTC twice, the audit-trail test asserts on the doubly converted value, and one log message has a typo. When she asked for the entity fix alone, the mapper and the test broke in new ways, and the next fix broke the entity again. What is the most effective way to proceed?
opcoes: Keep fixing one problem per message, but ask the agent to run the full test suite after each fix, so that any regression is caught as soon as it appears.
Regenerate the whole module from scratch with a longer prompt that lists all four problems, so that no fragment of the faulty version survives.
Describe all three time-handling problems together in one detailed message, since their fixes interact, and fix the unrelated log typo on its own.
Ask the agent to fix the audit-trail test first, since tests define the expected behavior, then let it adjust the entity and mapper until that test passes.
questoes.explicacao: When fixes interact, sequential iteration makes each change undo the previous one: the entity, the mapper and the test all encode the same timestamp contract. Describing the interacting problems together in one detailed message lets the agent change them consistently, while an independent issue such as the log typo is better handled separately. Matching the iteration style to whether problems interact is the key decision.
feedbacks: Running tests after each step detects regressions but does not prevent them: the three time problems are still fixed one at a time against an inconsistent contract, which is the loop she is already in.
Regenerating discards the parts that were fine and gives no guarantee that the new version handles time correctly; it rewrites too early instead of fixing the interacting issues together.
Correct. Interacting problems belong in one detailed message so the fixes stay consistent; the independent typo can be fixed separately.
Test-driven iteration works when the tests are right, but this test asserts the doubly converted value. Making the code pass it would lock the bug in.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, automates repetitive edits across the monorepo. Code under `validated/` belongs to GxP-validated systems, and policy requires a change request before any file there is modified. The system prompt says: 'Before writing to validated/, call open_change_request and put its ID in the commit message.' An audit of 900 runs found 31 in which the agent edited validated files without a change request, mostly small follow-up fixes late in long sessions. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Move the change-request rule to the top of the system prompt in capital letters and repeat it in the Write and Edit tool descriptions, so it stays salient.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks the Write and Edit tools on `validated/` paths until open_change_request has returned an ID in the current session.
Add few-shot examples of late-session follow-up fixes in which the agent calls open_change_request first, so that the model learns to follow this exact pattern.
Add a git post-commit hook that finds validated files committed without a change-request ID and reverts those commits, so violations do not persist.
questoes.explicacao: When compliance must be guaranteed, prompt instructions alone leave a non-zero failure rate, as the 31 violations show. A PreToolUse hook enforces the order programmatically: Write and Edit on `validated/` are blocked until a change request exists, however long the session runs. Prompt wording and examples can still help the agent plan, but they cannot be the control.
feedbacks: Making the instruction louder is still prompt-based guidance: it may lower the failure rate but cannot guarantee the order, and the policy needs a guarantee.
Correct. A programmatic prerequisite blocks the edit itself until the change request exists, which a prompt cannot guarantee.
Few-shot examples improve consistency but remain probabilistic; the agent can still skip the step in a situation the examples did not cover.
This is a hook, but it fires after the edit and commit, while policy requires the change request before modification. Reverting afterwards detects violations; it does not enforce the order.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, needs three new integrations: the company's GitHub organization, its Confluence wiki, and an in-house validation-evidence system that records which test runs support each GxP requirement. One engineer proposes writing a single custom MCP server that wraps all three APIs, 'so we control every tool description and error format'. Others suggest different splits. Which design is the best choice?
opcoes: Build the single custom server as proposed, since owning each tool lets the team keep descriptions and error formats consistent across the three systems.
Skip MCP for GitHub and Confluence and let the agent call their REST APIs with curl through Bash, building a custom server only for validation evidence.
Use community servers for GitHub and Confluence and reach validation evidence through a generic SQL MCP server, so that the team writes no server code.
Use existing community MCP servers for GitHub and Confluence, and build a custom server only for the in-house validation-evidence workflow.
questoes.explicacao: For standard integrations such as GitHub and Confluence, existing community MCP servers already provide maintained tools, so writing your own duplicates effort and maintenance. Custom servers are best reserved for team-specific workflows like the in-house validation-evidence system, where no existing server understands the domain. This mix gets the agent working fastest while keeping custom code where it adds value.
feedbacks: Consistency is a real benefit, but rebuilding GitHub and Confluence integrations that community servers already provide costs time and ongoing maintenance for little gain.
Raw curl through Bash gives the agent no tool descriptions, schemas or structured errors, so it trades a ready-made integration for a fragile one.
A generic SQL server exposes tables, not the team's workflow, so the agent would have to guess how evidence links to requirements. Team-specific workflows are what custom servers are for.
Correct. Use community servers for standard integrations and build custom ones only for team-specific workflows.

questoes.pergunta: At Corvane Pharma, engineers building the Agent SDK productivity tools use Claude Code to investigate the legacy LIMS before automating parts of it. One engineer is running three investigations over several days: sample lifecycle, label printing and instrument imports. Each morning she starts a new session and pastes her notes, and the agent re-reads 40–60 files it had already analyzed, although none of that code has changed. She wants each investigation to pick up exactly where it stopped, with its earlier analysis intact. What should she change?
opcoes: Give each investigation its own session name and continue it with `--resume <session-name>`, so that the matching conversation returns with all its analysis.
Keep one long session for all three investigations and run `/compact` each evening, so that a single conversation carries every finding forward.
Write each day's findings to a scratchpad file and start a fresh session that reads it, so that only the essential conclusions carry over into each new day.
Run `fork_session` from yesterday's session each morning, so that each investigation branches from a shared baseline without mixing their contexts.
questoes.explicacao: Named session resumption with `--resume <session-name>` restores a specific prior conversation, including the analysis already done. Because the code has not changed, that prior context is still valid, so resuming beats re-exploring. Starting fresh with a summary is the right choice only when earlier tool results have gone stale.
feedbacks: Correct. Named sessions plus `--resume` continue each investigation where it stopped, which suits context that is still valid.
Mixing three investigations in one session blurs their findings, and `/compact` replaces the history with a summary, losing the detailed analysis she wants to keep.
A summary in a fresh session is the right move when prior results are stale; here the code is unchanged, so it discards valid context the agent would have to rebuild.
`fork_session` creates divergent branches from a shared baseline to compare approaches; it does not keep three separate investigations going.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, explains legacy systems with a fixed four-step pipeline: Glob the module's source files, summarize each file, summarize the module's tests, then write an overview. For the pharmacovigilance intake module, the overview says case routing 'is driven by rules loaded from the ROUTING_RULES table and config/routing-2009.xml', but cannot say what any rule does or which of 17 stored procedures apply them. Engineers had to trace that by hand. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The fixed pipeline cannot add subtasks based on what it discovers, so leads such as the table and the XML file are noted but never investigated.
The per-file summaries are too short, so the details of the routing rules are lost before the overview step can combine them into an explanation.
The Glob pattern only matches source files, so the XML file and the stored procedures fall outside the set of files the pipeline was told to read.
The overview runs in the same context as all the per-file summaries, so attention dilution makes it skip the parts of the module that matter most.
questoes.explicacao: Open-ended investigation of a legacy system needs an adaptive plan that creates new subtasks from what each step uncovers. A fixed pipeline can only execute its predetermined steps, so when the router points to a table, an XML file and stored procedures, nothing follows those leads. Prompt chaining suits predictable multi-aspect work; exploring unknown code calls for dynamic decomposition.
feedbacks: Correct. Only an adaptive investigation plan turns discoveries such as the table and the XML file into new subtasks.
The overview did receive the details: it names both the table and the XML file. The gap is that no step ever looked into them.
Widening the Glob would add the XML file, but the procedures live in the database and the pipeline still would not know which rules matter. The real limit is that the steps are fixed in advance.
Attention dilution affects large single passes, but the overview reported the leads accurately. Nothing in the pipeline was designed to investigate them.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent uses a coordinator that spawns exploration subagents through the Task tool. To map where sample status changes in the LIMS, the coordinator sent: '1. Glob lims/sample/**/*.java. 2. Read the first 10 results. 3. Grep those files for setStatus. 4. Return the matching classes.' The subagent returned 6 classes. Engineers later found 9 more status transitions: in Kotlin files, in a SQL trigger and in a class that calls `updateState`. Every step had been executed as written. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: The subagent did not receive the coordinator's conversation history, so it could not know that status changes may also happen outside the Java code.
The subagent's tools should include Bash, so that it can run a full-text search over Kotlin, SQL and other file types in the repository, not just Java.
The prompt dictates a fixed procedure instead of the goal and what a complete answer must cover, so the subagent could not adapt when the code turned out to differ.
The coordinator should have spawned one subagent per file type in parallel, so that the Java, Kotlin and SQL searches would run independently.
questoes.explicacao: Coordinator prompts should state the research goal and the quality criteria for a complete answer, for example every status transition in any language, with file and line, and gaps flagged. A step-by-step recipe turns the subagent into a script runner: it obeyed every step, and the steps were wrong for this codebase. Goal-based prompts let subagents adapt their search when they meet Kotlin, SQL or differently named methods.
feedbacks: Subagents do need context passed explicitly, but the coordinator did not know about the Kotlin or SQL code either. The problem is that the prompt fixed the method instead of the goal.
Grep already searches any file type; the subagent did not lack a tool, it was told to Grep only 10 Java files for one method name.
Correct. Stating the goal and completeness criteria instead of a fixed procedure lets the subagent adapt to what it finds.
The coordinator could not have known in advance that Kotlin and SQL were involved, and parallel subagents with recipe-style prompts would still miss `updateState`.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, helps engineers map the legacy batch-record system. In version 1, a single agent ran every Grep and Read itself; after about 90 minutes its answers drifted toward 'typical repository patterns' instead of the classes it had found earlier. In version 2, the main agent sends specific questions such as 'find every caller of BatchRelease.approve' to subagents through the Task tool and keeps only their summaries; after 90 minutes its answers still cite specific classes. Which statement about this difference is correct?
opcoes: Version 2 works because subagents share the main agent's memory, so each finding is stored once and later questions can reuse it without new searches.
The verbose search and file output stays in each subagent's isolated context and only summaries return, so the main agent keeps room for the big picture.
Version 2 works mainly because the questions run in parallel, which shortens each session enough that the main agent does not reach the point where quality drops.
Version 1 would match version 2 with a model that has a larger context window, since the drift came from the window being too small for this system.
questoes.explicacao: Delegating specific questions to subagents isolates the verbose exploration output (hundreds of Grep hits and file contents) in their own contexts, while the main agent receives compact summaries and keeps coordinating at a high level. In version 1 that raw output accumulated in a single context until the model degraded into generic answers. Subagent delegation is a main lever against context degradation during large codebase exploration.
feedbacks: Subagents run with isolated context and do not share memory with the main agent; the benefit comes precisely from keeping their verbose work out of the main context.
Correct. Subagents absorb the verbose output and return summaries, so the main agent's context stays focused on high-level understanding.
Parallelism can cut wall-clock time, but the main agent ran for the same 90 minutes in both versions. What changed is what accumulated in its context.
A larger window delays the problem but does not remove it: the context still fills with raw output, and long inputs still suffer degraded attention.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, loads the repository's CLAUDE.md files and its project skills in `.claude/skills/`. The team has written a 380-line, nine-step procedure for scaffolding a new GxP-compliant service, used about twice a month. An engineer proposes pasting it into the root CLAUDE.md, next to universal rules such as 'all timestamps are UTC' and 'never log subject identifiers', 'so the agent always knows it'. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: CLAUDE.md is the one file the agent always reads, so it is the only place that ensures the procedure is followed whenever a service is scaffolded.
Reject it: package the procedure as a skill that is invoked on demand, and keep CLAUDE.md for universal standards that apply to every session.
Reject it: split the procedure into nine `.claude/rules/` files, one per step, so that each step loads only when the agent edits files matching its pattern.
Accept it, but move it into a directory-level CLAUDE.md inside the templates folder, so that it loads only when the agent is working in that folder.
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so it should hold standards that apply to every session, such as UTC timestamps and logging rules. A long, task-specific workflow used twice a month belongs in a skill, invoked on demand when someone scaffolds a service. Putting it in CLAUDE.md would spend context on every unrelated task without making it any more available when it is needed.
feedbacks: A skill is available whenever it is invoked, so CLAUDE.md is not the only way. Loading 380 lines into every session for a twice-a-month task wastes context on all the other work.
Correct. Skills fit on-demand, task-specific workflows; CLAUDE.md fits always-applicable standards.
Path-scoped rules fit conventions tied to file types or locations. A sequential procedure split into nine pattern-triggered files would load in fragments and lose its order.
Scaffolding creates a new service elsewhere in the repository, so a file tied to the templates folder may never load at the right moment. The workflow is task-driven, not location-driven.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent uses a coordinator that splits engineering questions into subtasks for subagents. Asked to assess the impact of retiring the legacy LIMS reporting module, it created two subtasks: 'find Java callers of ReportService' and 'list report templates'. Both subagents did their work well, and the final answer said retirement was safe. In staging, a nightly data-warehouse ETL, three scheduled export jobs and a QA spreadsheet that pulls report URLs all broke. Which conclusions follow? Choose TWO.
opcoes: The coordinator should first list every kind of consumer, such as jobs, ETL and external tools, then assign and check each one before concluding.
Grep-based search is unreliable for impact analysis, so the subagents should read every file in the repository instead of searching for callers.
The subagents' summaries were too short, so their findings about the ETL and the scheduled jobs were lost before the coordinator combined them.
The coordinator's decomposition covered only in-repo Java callers and templates, so whole classes of consumers were never assigned to any subagent.
The subagents should have noticed the missing consumers and widened their own scope, so their prompts need an instruction to search beyond the assigned task.
questoes.explicacao: The subagents did exactly what they were asked; the gap lies in what they were asked. A decomposition that is too narrow leaves whole areas of a broad question uncovered, so the coordinator should enumerate the categories the question spans before delegating and verify coverage of each. Blaming downstream agents for not exceeding their assignment misplaces the fault.
feedbacks: Correct. Enumerating consumer categories before delegating, then checking each, is how a coordinator avoids overly narrow decomposition.
Reading every file is costly and would still be limited to the repository; the ETL, jobs and spreadsheet were never part of any subagent's assignment.
There were no such findings to lose: no subagent was asked to look at the ETL or the scheduled jobs.
Correct. The coordinator's narrow decomposition left the ETL, jobs and external tools without any subagent assigned.
Asking subagents to roam beyond their tasks creates overlap and unpredictable scope. Coverage is the coordinator's job when it decomposes the question.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, has an MCP tool `search_change_history` whose description explains in detail that it returns change-control records, validation status and approvers for any module. The agent's system prompt also says: 'When the user asks about history, run git log through Bash.' For 41 of 50 logged questions such as 'what is the validation history of the dosing module?', the agent ran git log and answered from commit messages. Which actions best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add more example queries to the `search_change_history` description, so that it outweighs the instruction about history in the system prompt.
Review the system prompt for other keyword-triggered instructions that tie words such as 'history' or 'search' to one specific tool.
Remove Bash from the agent's tools, so that git log can no longer be chosen when engineers ask questions about a module's history.
Rewrite the 'history' instruction to explain when git log fits and when the change-control tool fits, instead of keying on any single word.
Force `search_change_history` with tool_choice whenever a message contains 'validation', so the right tool is the one that runs first.
questoes.explicacao: The tool description is already good; the system prompt's keyword rule ('history' means git log) overrides it. Keyword-sensitive instructions create unintended tool associations, so the fix is to rewrite that rule around the actual distinction and to audit the prompt for similar rules. Adding description text or routing by other keywords leaves the conflict in place.
feedbacks: The description is already detailed; more examples would still compete with an explicit system-prompt rule that names a different tool.
Correct. Auditing the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions finds other rules that may override good tool descriptions.
Bash is needed for builds and other automation, and git log is the right tool for commit history. Removing it breaks valid uses instead of fixing the conflicting rule.
Correct. Replacing the keyword trigger with the real distinction lets the descriptions and the prompt point the same way.
This swaps one keyword rule for another and forces a tool even when 'validation' appears in an unrelated question.

questoes.pergunta: At Corvane Pharma, an engineer prototyping a boilerplate generator for the team's developer-productivity tools wrote a small agentic loop on the Messages API before porting it to the Claude Agent SDK. When `stop_reason` is "tool_use", the loop runs the tool, then sends a new request containing the original user message plus the latest tool result. In tests, the agent repeats the same Grep up to four times and generates classes that ignore files it had already read. Which statements are correct? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Every tool result must be appended to the conversation after the assistant turn that requested it, so the model can see what it did and what came back.
Because the loop drops earlier tool calls and results, the model has no record of its previous searches, which explains the repeated Grep calls.
Instead of resending earlier turns, the loop should replace them after each iteration with a short summary, so requests stay small and focused.
The tool results are probably too verbose; trimming each Grep and Read result to its first 20 lines would stop the model from repeating its searches.
The repeated calls show the loop needs a fixed iteration cap, since the model cannot judge by itself when it has explored enough of the code.
questoes.explicacao: The Messages API is stateless: the model knows only what is in the request. The loop must append the assistant's tool_use turn and the matching tool result to the conversation history and send that full history on each iteration, so the model can reason about what it already tried. Dropping earlier turns makes it repeat searches and forget files it has read.
feedbacks: Correct. Appending each tool result after the turn that requested it is how the model incorporates new information into its next decision.
Correct. With earlier calls and results dropped, the model cannot know it already ran that Grep or read those files.
Replacing turns with summaries discards the exact results and file contents the generator needs, and the model loses the record of which calls it already made.
Trimming verbose results helps the context budget, but the model repeats searches because it never sees its earlier calls; shorter results would not bring them back.
An iteration cap would only cut the loop short; the repeats come from missing history, and caps are not a sound primary stopping mechanism.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent has a coordinator and three subagents: an explorer (Read, Grep, Glob), a generator (Read, Write, Edit) and a runner (Bash). Before writing boilerplate, the generator must check whether a class or file name already exists; this happens in 70% of tasks, and each check goes through the coordinator to the explorer, adding about 25 seconds. Deeper questions, such as tracing a dependency chain, are rare. The team wants fewer round trips without the generator running builds or broad investigations. What should they change?
opcoes: Give the generator the explorer's full tool set, so that it can answer any code question by itself and the coordinator no longer has to route exploration requests.
Merge the explorer and the generator into one subagent with Read, Write, Edit, Grep and Glob, so that exploration and generation share a single context.
Give the generator a scoped `name_exists` tool for the frequent collision check, and keep routing all deeper questions through the coordinator to the explorer.
Have the explorer list every class and file name at the start of each task and pass it to the generator, so that name checks never need a tool call.
questoes.explicacao: Scoped tool access gives each agent only the tools its role needs, plus narrow cross-role tools for high-frequency needs. A `name_exists` check covers the 70% case directly, while the rarer, complex investigations still go through the coordinator to the explorer. This removes most round trips without turning the generator into a general-purpose agent.
feedbacks: Full exploration tools invite the generator to run broad investigations, which the team wants to avoid, and more tools make tool selection less reliable.
Merging roles removes the specialization that keeps each agent's tool set small and focused, and exploration output would crowd the generator's context.
Correct. A narrow cross-role tool handles the frequent check, while complex cases keep flowing through the coordinator.
Pre-listing every name in a large monorepo floods the generator's context and goes stale as soon as new files are created; it is speculative pre-fetching.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, answers questions such as 'how does a sample get released in the LIMS?'. Session logs show that it starts with a Glob for `lims/**/*.java` (2,300 files) and then calls Read on the files in path order. After about 140 files the context fills up, earlier details are compacted, and the final answer describes a generic approval flow that omits `ReleaseGate`, the class that enforces QA sign-off. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The agent reads files wholesale instead of using Grep to find the release entry points and then reading only the files those entry points lead to.
Glob returns files in path order, so the important ones come late; sorting the Glob results by modification date would surface the relevant files much sooner.
The context window is too small for a module of 2,300 files; a model with a larger window would hold the whole module at once and so find `ReleaseGate`.
The agent should load files in batches with `cat` through Bash, which fits far more content into context than individual Read calls do.
questoes.explicacao: Effective codebase exploration is incremental: Grep for entry points such as `releaseSample` or 'QA sign-off', then Read those files and follow their imports and calls. Reading files upfront in path order fills the context with irrelevant code long before reaching the classes that matter. Grep finds content and Glob finds paths; neither should be a prelude to reading everything.
feedbacks: Correct. Starting with Grep to find entry points and then following imports with Read builds understanding without flooding the context.
A different order is still a guess: the agent would keep reading unrelated files, and recently modified files are not necessarily the relevant ones.
Even a larger window would fill with mostly irrelevant code, and long inputs suffer degraded attention. The strategy, not the window, is the problem.
`cat` output consumes context just like Read; batching changes nothing about reading the wrong files upfront.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent uses a custom MCP server, `lims-db`, whose `run_readonly_query` tool lets engineers inspect legacy schemas. When a query fails, the server catches the exception and returns a normal tool result whose text is the database message, for example `permission denied for schema qa_private`. In one session, the agent reported that `qa_private.deviations` 'has a single text column' and then generated a repository class for that table. What is the flaw in the server's implementation?
opcoes: The server should let the exception escape so that the MCP connection fails and the agent stops before it generates code from bad data.
The server should return an empty result set when a query fails, so that the agent does not mistake the database message for column data.
The tool description should tell the agent to treat results that start with an error keyword as failures, so the model can filter those out itself.
Failures come back as ordinary results without the `isError` flag, so the agent has no reliable signal that the call failed and reads the message as data.
questoes.explicacao: MCP tools report failures by setting `isError: true` on the result, ideally with structured details such as the error category and whether a retry makes sense. Without the flag, an error message looks exactly like a successful result, so the agent treated 'permission denied' as table content. Flagging the error lets the agent recognize the failure and choose to report it, try another schema or ask for access.
feedbacks: Crashing the connection aborts the whole session over one failed query and gives the agent nothing to reason about; a flagged error lets it recover.
An empty result looks like a successful query that matched nothing, which hides the permission problem: that is silent suppression of the error.
Asking the model to parse error wording is fragile and probabilistic; the protocol already provides a dedicated flag for this signal.
Correct. Without `isError`, the agent cannot tell a failed call from a successful one and treats the error text as data.

questoes.pergunta: Corvane Pharma's developer-productivity agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, is configured with three MCP servers: `lims-db`, `change-control` and `confluence`. An engineer asks why a validated LIMS table changed last spring. In a single response, the agent calls `search_requests` from the change-control server and `describe_table` from the lims-db server, then cites a Confluence design page. A teammate expected the agent to work with one server at a time and asks whether a routing layer is involved. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The tools of every configured MCP server are discovered when the agent connects and offered together, so the model can use several servers' tools in one turn.
The SDK activates one MCP server per turn based on the user's wording, and both servers were used here only because the question named both systems.
There must be a coordinator routing each request to a per-server subagent, since an agent can only hold a connection to one MCP server at a time.
MCP servers are connected lazily on the first call to one of their tools, so the Confluence server started only after the agent chose to cite the page.
questoes.explicacao: When the agent starts, it connects to every configured MCP server and discovers their tools, which are then available simultaneously alongside the built-in tools. No routing layer is needed: in each turn the model picks among all available tools, guided by their descriptions. This is also why clear, distinct descriptions matter more as servers are added.
feedbacks: Correct. All configured servers' tools are discovered at connection time and available to the agent at once.
There is no per-turn activation by wording; every configured server's tools are available in every turn.
A single agent can connect to many MCP servers at once; per-server subagents are a design choice, not a requirement.
Tools are discovered when the agent connects, not lazily; the Confluence tools were already available before the agent decided to use them.

questoes.pergunta: At Corvane Pharma, engineers building the Agent SDK productivity tools use Claude Code to map the legacy LIMS before automating parts of it. One engineer has a named session, `audit-trail-map`, in which the agent analyzed 48 files over two days. Since then, a merged pull request changed 3 of those files: `AuditWriter.java`, `AuditEvent.java` and one migration script. She proposes resuming with `--resume audit-trail-map` and first telling the agent which three files changed and how. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: most of the earlier analysis is still valid, and naming the changed files lets the agent re-analyze just those instead of trusting stale results.
Accept the resume but skip the note: the agent re-reads files whenever it needs them, so its earlier findings about those files will refresh themselves automatically.
Reject it: resuming on top of stale tool results is unreliable, so she should start a new session and inject a structured summary of the earlier findings.
Reject it: she should run `fork_session` from the old session, so that the changed files are analyzed in a branch that cannot affect the original.
questoes.explicacao: Resuming is the right choice when prior context is mostly valid, as here with 45 of 48 files unchanged. The agent does not know the code changed, though, so telling it exactly which files changed lets it re-analyze them in a targeted way instead of reasoning from stale tool results or re-exploring everything. Starting fresh with an injected summary is the better choice when most earlier tool results are stale.
feedbacks: Correct. Resume when context is mostly valid, and point the agent at the specific changed files for targeted re-analysis.
The agent has no reason to re-read files it believes it has already analyzed; without the note, it keeps reasoning from the old contents.
That is the right move when most prior results are stale, but only 3 of 48 files changed here, so discarding the session wastes valid analysis.
`fork_session` is for exploring divergent approaches from a shared baseline; it does not tell the agent which files changed.
